hero.headline.text: Before you send out more agents,

hero.takeaway.text: Do the same question-writing task four ways, as a single agent, a fixed workflow, role switching and independent agents, and hand every result to the same program verifier. Whether the split buys new information or only more calls, the ledger and the verdict will tell you.

concepts.01-one-context.description.text: The single agent puts the task, the rule and all four documents into one request. It is the baseline: a split only pays off if it beats this.

concepts.02-shared.description.text: One run identity puts on the researcher, writer and reviewer system prompts in turn, and every earlier message is still there.

concepts.03-isolated.description.text: Each researcher gets only the documents assigned to it, and the requests go out in parallel, each with its own branch; the writer and the reviewer also start from an empty message list.

concepts.04-same-check.description.text: The final questions of all four modes go to verify_quiz: the evidence must be found word for word, must not come from the old draft, and the correct option must state the documented value.

section-1.paragraphs.0.text: Multi-agent systems add call and coordination costs, so you need evidence that a split pays off. {{lesson:workflow-patterns}} and {{lesson:orchestrator-evaluator}} already split one task across several model calls: prompt chaining, routing, orchestrator-workers and evaluator-optimizer. All of those calls stay under one runner: who goes first and what each one sees is written in the program. This lesson goes one step further and asks whether several agents, each with its own identity and its own context, are worth it.

section-1.paragraphs.1.text: Start with the bill. Done by a single agent, this lesson's task is 1 request; split into three researchers, a writer and a reviewer, it is 5 requests. Every request repeats the task description and the format requirements, so the input adds up to several times that of the single request. Parallelism lets the three researchers wait at the same time and may shorten the wall-clock time, but the number of model calls and the usage do not drop by a single call. Those extra calls only pay off if they buy something the single agent cannot get.

section-1.paragraphs.2.text: Understanding AI Agents in Depth gives a single test: does the collaboration bring in information that a single agent could not have had while generating? A reviewer who reviews with test results, rendered screenshots or facts looked up with a tool brings new information, and the effect is usually clear; the same model rereading its own output under another identity brings none, and often just costs money. Two other reasons also hold up: the material is too large for one context, or several pieces of work are independent and running them in parallel saves waiting time.

section-1.paragraphs.3.text: So the number of agents is not a measure of capability. This lesson does not assume a winner: the four modes do the same task and go to the same program verifier, and the report puts pass or fail, the number of model calls, the usage the provider reported and the wall-clock time side by side. When the multi-agent mode does not produce a better result, or goes over the call budget, staying with a single agent is the sensible choice.

section-2.paragraphs.0.text: Manager, peer and hierarchical organizations each suit different tasks. In the manager pattern a central role reads the task, splits it into subtasks, sends them out, collects the results and puts them together; the orchestrator in {{lesson:orchestrator-evaluator}} is a simplified version. In this lesson's independent-agents mode the manager is simply the program: how the documents are split, when the researchers are sent out in parallel and how the facts are merged are all decided in code, without a single model call.

section-2.paragraphs.1.text: In the peer pattern two or three agents of equal standing give each other feedback, for example one drafts and one annotates, for a few rounds. It is the simplest to build; the hard parts are the stop condition and diversity: with the same model and similar contexts, several colleagues often think alike, and agreeing with each other is not independent verification. In the hierarchical pattern managers sit under a manager, which suits large tasks whose subtasks must be split again, for example translating a book by giving chapters to a few team leads who hand them on to translators; every extra level adds another link where messages can get garbled.

section-2.paragraphs.2.text: One more approach is often mistaken for multi-agent: the fixed workflow. In the prompt chain of {{lesson:workflow-patterns}}, each step is a fresh request whose input the program picks, and the order is hard-coded. This lesson's fixed workflow also has research, writing and review steps, but no step decides what happens next; it is a workflow. This lesson treats it as a second baseline: when a fixed workflow already passes the acceptance set, there is no need to let a model coordinate.

section-2.paragraphs.3.text: To choose, look at the shape of the task first. Fixed steps with clear inputs for each: use a workflow. Subtasks you can only split after reading the input: use the manager pattern. One output that needs repeated polishing, with criteria you can state: use a peer write-and-review loop. Only when subtasks must be split again and the scale is too much for one manager, consider the hierarchical pattern. Each step along this list adds coordination cost and more places to fail, so start with the simplest and move up only when you have evidence.

deep-dive-taxonomy.title.text: Two dimensions: is context shared, and how does control flow?

deep-dive-taxonomy.summary.text: Understanding AI Agents in Depth classifies multi-agent collaboration along these two dimensions, and all four of this lesson's modes fit in.

deep-dive-taxonomy.paragraphs.0.text: The first dimension is whether context is shared. With shared context, each later stage inherits the whole message history before it and only swaps the system prompt and tools, like a colleague taking over a shift who can read every work note of the one before; this lesson's role switching belongs here. Without shared context, each agent has its own message history and cannot see the other's reasoning; information passes only through tool arguments, shared files or a message bus. This lesson's independent agents belong here, and what passes between them is JSON the program has prepared.

deep-dive-taxonomy.paragraphs.1.text: The second dimension is the collaboration topology: peer, manager or decentralized. A decentralized system has no central role; agents decide for themselves whom to hand work to, which the microservices world calls choreography, as opposed to the orchestration of the manager pattern. The book also compares a multi-agent system with an operating system: the system prompt plus tool definitions is like a program, the trace like a process's memory, sending out a subagent like creating a child process, and the summary a subagent returns like an exit code. The analogy is a reminder that the benefits of process isolation (no cross-contamination, parallel execution) arrive together with its costs (explicit communication, piecing several logs together when debugging).

deep-dive-taxonomy.paragraphs.2.text: Who matters most in the manager pattern? The Plan-and-Act study the book cites found that the planner's quality is the bottleneck of the whole system: if the split is wrong, every executor after it works on a wrong premise. So resources should not be spread evenly; the strongest model and the most careful prompt belong to whoever splits and assembles the work. In this lesson the manager is a program with a fixed split: the split itself cannot go wrong, but however clumsy it is, it will never change by itself, and the experiment below shows one example.

misconception-more-agents.claim.text: The more agents and the finer the roles, the stronger the system.

misconception-more-agents.correction.text: The number of roles is not a measure of capability. Every extra agent means another request, another copy of the prompt and another handoff of information; the same model reviewing itself under another identity often just costs more when no new information comes in. Whether a split pays off has to be compared with a single agent on the same task and the same verifier, reporting the extra calls at the same time.

predict-calls.prompt.text: Before you run "Independent agents", guess: how many request events will this run have?

mq-parallel-cost.parallel-cost.prompt.text: In this lesson the single-agent mode is 1 request and the independent-agents mode is 5 requests, with three researchers in parallel. Which statement is right?

mq-parallel-cost.parallel-cost.a.text.text: Parallelism may shorten the wall-clock time, but model calls and usage still count all 5

mq-parallel-cost.parallel-cost.a.feedbac.text: Right. Parallelism saves waiting, not calls.

mq-parallel-cost.parallel-cost.b.text.text: The three parallel requests count as one for usage

mq-parallel-cost.parallel-cost.b.feedbac.text: No. Every request is metered on its own.

mq-parallel-cost.parallel-cost.c.text.text: 5 requests always write more accurate questions than 1

mq-parallel-cost.parallel-cost.c.feedbac.text: No. The extra calls only help if they bring new information, and the verifier still has to check.

mq-parallel-cost.parallel-cost.explanati.text: Time and cost are two different things; report them separately.

section-3.title.text: Role switching: a new prompt, not a new context

section-3.paragraphs.0.text: Role switching means one agent puts on a different system prompt while the message history stays shared; it is not a second agent. Look at the three requests of this lesson's role-switching mode: the first system prompt says you are a researcher, the second switches to a writer, the third to a reviewer. Apart from that first system message, not a single message is dropped, and the previous stage's reply stays in place word for word. In the lesson.agent events of the three requests the run identity is always assistant; only the role changes.

section-3.paragraphs.1.text: It is like one person wearing three hats in turn. With the reviewer's hat on, they still remember what they read as a researcher and why they wrote the questions the way they did as a writer. The benefit is that nothing is lost: the review stage can find the exact text the research stage found. The cost is in the same place: the context grows each round, and the third request carries every reply from the two earlier stages; the reviewer and the writer share one line of thought, so reviewing yourself rarely catches a shared blind spot.

section-3.paragraphs.2.text: So to tell whether a system really has several agents, check three things instead of counting role names in the prompts: are the contexts separate, are the tools each one can use different, and are the run identities different. This lesson's ledger records, call by call, the run identity, the role, the number of messages, the input characters and which documents were seen. The book also compares another way of switching roles: keep the system prompt fixed and load a skill description on demand. That keeps the stable prefix and makes use of prompt caching, but out-of-scope tools stay visible, and hard permissions must be enforced separately by the harness.

section-4.paragraphs.0.text: A subagent sees only the context it needs, which cuts out distractions and also loses information. Context isolation means each agent starts from an empty message list and holds only what is handed to it. In the independent-agents mode, the manager (the program) sends out three subagents as researchers: researcher-1 sees only d1, researcher-2 only d2, and researcher-3 sees d3 and d4. The three requests go out at the same time, each with its own branch, and the timeline pairs requests and responses by it.

section-4.paragraphs.1.text: You can work out the benefit by hand. The single agent has to read four documents and keep the format requirements in mind in one context before writing; after the split, each researcher's input is just one or two documents, and the writer does not read the documents at all, only the merged list of facts. With more material the difference becomes large: {{lesson:context-budget}} showed that information in the window is not necessarily used, and the shorter the input, the easier it is for the model to focus on the few sentences that matter. The subagent example in the Learn Claude Code tutorial follows the same idea: a subagent may read dozens of files, and the parent gets back only a short conclusion.

section-4.paragraphs.2.text: The cost is that a subagent knows nothing that was not handed over. This lesson's task description contains a rule: d4 is an old draft and must not be used as evidence when it conflicts with the other documents. The single agent, the fixed workflow and role switching all have this rule in their contexts; with the minimal handoff, the independent researchers get only the task and their assigned documents, and the rule is not passed on. In researcher-3's lesson.agent event, outdated_docs lists d4 while sees_rule is false: it holds the old draft without knowing it is old.

section-4.paragraphs.3.text: The isolation here is message isolation only: the three researchers run in one process and share one model connection and one call budget, with parallel requests counted under the platform's lock. They have no working directories of their own and no different tools. In real systems isolation often also covers files, permissions and a budget per subagent, which {{lesson:delegation-budget}} takes up next.

deep-dive-real-systems.title.text: Subagents and teams in real systems

deep-dive-real-systems.summary.text: From one-off subagents to long-lived teammates, there is more and more to isolate and to agree on.

deep-dive-real-systems.paragraphs.0.text: The Learn Claude Code tutorial covers this in two steps. The first is the subagent: the parent agent has a tool for dispatching tasks, and the dispatched subagent starts from an empty message list and runs its own tool loop for at most 30 rounds; when it finishes, only its last piece of text is returned and the whole intermediate process is discarded. A subagent cannot dispatch subagents of its own, which prevents endless recursion. The tutorial points out that this is only message isolation: parent and child share one working directory, so writing files and running commands still affect each other.

deep-dive-real-systems.paragraphs.1.text: The second step is the team. Teammates are long-lived, with names and states, switching between working and idle, and they message each other through one inbox file per person. The lead first proposes a division of work and waits for the user's confirmation before actually sending teammates out, because every extra teammate is another cost and another role that can change the workspace; when parallel changes might touch the same files, tasks get separate working copies. What this step adds beyond this lesson is exactly identity, lifecycle and a communication protocol.

deep-dive-real-systems.paragraphs.2.text: A team example in Claude Cookbooks adds something that is easy to miss: the team shares one clock, and before every call the elapsed seconds are appended to the end of the newest message, so a teammate sent out late sees the team's time rather than starting from zero; the budget sits on the same clock, and the whole team paces itself by it.

deep-dive-real-systems.paragraphs.3.text: Claude Code works in a similar way: the model in the main conversation can hand subtasks to agents working in contexts of their own, each with its own system prompt and available tools, and they return only a summary when done; independent investigations can be sent out several at a time, and each one uses usage of its own; see the official documentation for the exact mechanism. An Anthropic multi-agent study also reported a comparison: in an open-ended vulnerability search, 45 agents that communicated and coordinated used about 27 million tokens to find 266 vulnerabilities, while a setup of independent agents in parallel used about 6.5 million tokens to find 21. The gain is real, and so is a cost several times higher; the numbers are as reported in the original, and they may not hold for another task.

mq-role-identity.role-identity.prompt.text: The role-switching mode made 3 requests, and the ledger shows only one run identity, assistant. What does that tell you?

mq-role-identity.role-identity.a.text.text: The three stages are one agent swapping system prompts with a shared message history, not three independent agents

mq-role-identity.role-identity.a.feedbac.text: Right. The role changed; the context and the run identity were not separated.

mq-role-identity.role-identity.b.text.text: The platform merged the identities of three agents for display

mq-role-identity.role-identity.b.feedbac.text: No. The runner records run identities from the actual calls.

mq-role-identity.role-identity.c.text.text: The contexts of the three stages are isolated from each other

mq-role-identity.role-identity.c.feedbac.text: No. The second and third requests both carry the earlier stages' replies.

mq-role-identity.role-identity.explanati.text: To tell whether there are several agents, look at contexts, tools and run identities, not at the role names in the prompts.

section-5.title.text: The handoff package and three failures

section-5.paragraphs.0.text: Independent agents pass information only through handoff packages, and whatever a handoff package leaves out turns into context loss, duplicated work and contradictions. The handoff package that Understanding AI Agents in Depth describes usually has three parts: what the receiver must do and what the acceptance criteria are; the facts and constraints already confirmed; references to the artifacts. This lesson's minimal handoff has only the first part plus the documents; the handoff with rules adds the constraint that d4 is out of date, and the parameter handoff switches between them.

section-5.paragraphs.1.text: See what happens with the minimal handoff. researcher-2 finds in d2 that the subtask limit is 4; researcher-3 does not know d4 is out of date and finds 6 in it. Two researchers looked up the same topic, which is duplicated work; they found two different values, which is a contradiction. At the merge, merge_facts records both in lesson.merge: duplicates contains worker_cap, and conflicts lists both sources. The program only records and does not decide, because if it picked a value for the researchers, it would quietly hide the rule inside the merge code.

section-5.paragraphs.2.text: Next comes the cascade. The writer gets only the merged facts and no rule either; in offline test mode the script makes it take the later fact and write a question from d4. A real model may choose right or wrong, so look at your own run. The reviewer is independent and sees only the draft and the documents the draft cites; the quote really is copied word for word from d4, so it finds no problem. Finally the program verifier, applying the full rules, fails this question: the evidence comes from the old draft, and the correct option is not the documented value 4. Run again with the handoff with rules: researcher-3 no longer reports the value from d4, the conflict and the duplicate disappear, and the price is an extra paragraph of rules in every subagent's input.

section-5.paragraphs.3.text: All three failures can be found in the events, no guessing needed: context loss in sees_rule of lesson.agent, duplicated work and contradictions in lesson.merge, and the final consequence in the verifier's checks. Nor are they peculiar to multi-agent systems; a fixed workflow can also lose information at a handoff. The difference is that more subagents mean more handoffs and more chances to lose something, and every retelling is a lossy restatement.

misconception-reviewer.claim.text: Add an independent reviewer agent and it will catch the earlier agents' mistakes.

misconception-reviewer.correction.text: A reviewer can only check what it can see. This lesson's reviewer did not get the rule that d4 is out of date, and the quote really is copied word for word from d4, so it lets the question through. An independent view only helps when paired with real new information, such as rules, test results or facts looked up with a tool; final acceptance still belongs to the program verifier, which knows the full rules.

section-6.title.text: Comparing on the same question set

section-6.paragraphs.0.text: A single agent, a fixed workflow and multiple agents are compared on quality and cost over the same question set. This lesson's set is small: four documents and three topics, with the acceptance set written as the program verify_quiz, which checks four things per topic: exactly one question; correct format; the quote appears word for word in the document it names, and that document is not d4; the correct option states the documented value, and no other option does. The runner calls it the same way for the final questions of all four modes, and the events mark it as a call initiated by the runner.

section-6.paragraphs.1.text: Read a few numbers side by side in the report. Task acceptance: how many of the three topics passed. Model calls: 1, 3, 3 and 5 for the four modes. Total total_tokens: only numbers the provider reported are added; if none were reported it says not reported, and if some were missing it says how many. Wall-clock time: measured on the backend from the start to the last response; in the independent-agents mode the three researchers run in parallel and this stretch overlaps. Also look at the total input characters: role switching's context grows each round, so this figure is usually larger than the fixed workflow's.

section-6.paragraphs.2.text: Hold on to three rules when reading the results. First, only compare results on the same task and the same verifier; once the questions or the acceptance criteria change, the numbers cannot be put side by side. Second, one run is one sample: {{lesson:sampling-variance}} showed that the same request can come back different each time, so before drawing a conclusion run each mode several times and keep the failure records, as {{lesson:evaluation-sets}} does. Third, even for a multi-agent mode that passes, ask: what new information did the calls beyond the single agent buy? If you cannot say, stay with a single agent.

section-6.paragraphs.3.text: {{lesson:delegation-budget}} goes on to delegation itself: how the main agent writes the handoff package, how the results a subagent returns are merged into the main context, and how each subagent's budget is set. This lesson first establishes how to judge: a split is a design choice that has to be proven with data, not a more advanced way of writing by default. Before you run anything, write down your prediction: which mode costs most, which is most likely to go wrong and at which step, then compare with the report afterwards.

deep-dive-failures.title.text: Why multi-agent systems fail: findings from a few studies

deep-dive-failures.summary.text: Failures mostly come from design, alignment and acceptance, not just from a model that is not clever enough.

deep-dive-failures.paragraphs.0.text: The 2025 paper Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? collected execution traces from 7 mainstream frameworks, had people analyze about 150 of them one by one, and identified 14 failure modes in three groups: system design flaws, such as unclear interface definitions and overlapping role responsibilities; misalignment between agents, such as different understandings of the goal, information misread after being passed on, and actions that contradict each other; and missing task verification, where an agent says it is done but the result does not actually pass. Simple fixes helped little, and the researchers concluded that the problem lies in the architecture itself.

deep-dive-failures.paragraphs.1.text: Distributed systems divide faults into two kinds: crash faults, where a component simply stops working, and Byzantine faults, where a component keeps working but gives wrong information. Agent faults are mostly the second kind: an agent rarely stops; it keeps giving plausible wrong conclusions, and the error does not announce itself. This lesson's researcher-3 is a case in point: it raised no error and dutifully returned a value from d4. Such faults are countered by an independent view cross-checked against the original evidence, not by more agents thinking along the same line once more.

deep-dive-failures.paragraphs.2.text: Another failure comes from sameness. In an experiment the book cites, 18 of 30 agents launched at the same time created branches with the same name: the same model in similar contexts makes the same choice in the same place and the same mistake. So several reviews from the same model cannot count as several independent pieces of evidence; real diversity means deliberately varying the model, the context, the tools or the visible evidence, and letting each agent judge independently before results are combined. At the other extreme is the loop that will not stop: a runaway agent may send out hundreds or thousands of subagents, which is exactly why this lesson hard-codes the dispatching in the program and caps the calls for the whole run.

mq-cascade.cascade.prompt.text: With the minimal handoff, the independent reviewer let the question citing d4 through. What is the root cause?

mq-cascade.cascade.a.text.text: The reviewer's handoff package lacks the rule that d4 is out of date, and the quote really is copied word for word from d4

mq-cascade.cascade.a.feedback.text: Right. It can only check what it can see.

mq-cascade.cascade.b.text.text: The reviewer and the writer use the same run identity

mq-cascade.cascade.b.feedback.text: No. The reviewer has its own run identity and context.

mq-cascade.cascade.c.text.text: The verifier does not check document sources

mq-cascade.cascade.c.feedback.text: No. The verifier knows the full rules; it is what failed the question.

mq-cascade.cascade.explanation.text: A constraint the handoff package leaves out is missing for every agent downstream; acceptance that knows the full rules has to catch it at the end.

walkthrough.title.text: One run of the independent agents

walkthrough.description.text: A step-by-step account of one run with the minimal handoff; the code is a simplified sketch. The evidence of your own run is in the events on the lab bench.

walkthrough.step-1.title.text: Send out three researchers in parallel, one shard each

walkthrough.step-1.body.text: Each request carries its own branch, and its context holds only the assigned documents.

walkthrough.step-2.title.text: Merge the facts, record duplicates and conflicts

walkthrough.step-2.body.text: Two researchers reported different values for worker_cap; the program records it and decides nothing for them.

walkthrough.step-3.title.text: Write in a new context, then review independently

walkthrough.step-3.body.text: The writer sees only the merged facts; the reviewer sees only the draft and the documents it cites.

walkthrough.step-4.title.text: Hand it to the same verifier

walkthrough.step-4.body.text: Each topic is checked against the full rules, and the result goes into the lab report.

code-modes.n-single.text.text: Single agent: one context holds the task, the rule and all documents, in just 1 request.

code-modes.n-single-brief.text.text: The second argument of brief says whether the rule is included. The first three modes always pass True.

code-modes.n-workflow.text.text: Fixed workflow: the order is hard-coded in the program, and each step is a fresh request.

code-modes.n-workflow-research.text.text: The research step returns only the list of facts; its line of thought is not passed to the next step.

code-modes.n-workflow-write.text.text: The program picks the writing step's input: task, rule and facts, no documents.

code-modes.n-workflow-review.text.text: The review step gets all documents again, plus the draft.

code-modes.n-workflow-final.text.text: The reviewer's list is final; when it returns no list, the draft goes to the verifier as it was.

code-modes.n-roles.text.text: Role switching: one run identity, one message history.

code-modes.n-roles-stages.text.text: Only the first user message carries the documents and the rule; the two later stages see them through the shared history.

code-modes.n-roles-loop.text.text: Each pass of the loop is one stage, and the stage number is the request's round.

code-modes.n-roles-swap.text.text: Only the first system message changes; the run identity stays assistant, and in the ledger only the role changes.

code-modes.n-roles-history.text.text: The reply goes back into the same history, so the next role reads it in full, and the context grows every round.

code-modes.n-roles-final.text.text: The same closing rule as the fixed workflow, so the two modes differ only in how context is passed.

code-multi.n-merge.text.text: The program does the merge; it costs no model call.

code-multi.n-merge-filter.text.text: Only facts for the three topics are kept; malformed entries are skipped.

code-multi.n-merge-agent.text.text: Each fact carries the run identity of its source, so a conflict shows who reported what.

code-multi.n-merge-dup.text.text: A topic reported by more than one researcher: duplicated work.

code-multi.n-merge-conflict.text.text: Different values for the same topic: a contradiction, with every source listed.

code-multi.n-merge-return.text.text: Record, do not decide: every fact is passed on as it is.

code-multi.n-multi.text.text: rules comes from the parameter handoff: whether the handoff package includes the rule that d4 is out of date.

code-multi.n-multi-research.text.text: One researcher is one independent request: a new message list with only its own shard.

code-multi.n-multi-branch.text.text: The run identity and the branch are both the researcher's name, such as researcher-3.

code-multi.n-multi-pool.text.text: The three researchers go out in parallel and share one call budget.

code-multi.n-multi-merge.text.text: The merge happens only after every researcher has returned, and its result is recorded as lesson.merge.

code-multi.n-multi-writer.text.text: The writer's context: the handoff plus the merged facts, with neither the documents nor the research process.

code-multi.n-multi-cited.text.text: The reviewer gets only the documents the draft cites.

code-multi.n-multi-review.text.text: The reviewer also starts from a new context and cannot see the writer's reasoning: that is the independent view.

code-multi.n-multi-return.text.text: The final list and the merge record go back to the runner, which calls the verifier.

code-multi.fold-merge-event.label.text: Platform: publish the merge event lesson.merge

code-verifier.n-check.text.text: Checks one question and returns problem codes; an empty list means it passed.

code-verifier.n-check-format.text.text: A malformed question stops here, so bad data does not produce a string of follow-on errors.

code-verifier.n-check-evidence.text.text: The evidence is a document id plus the exact text; the verifier goes back to the documents to check it itself.

code-verifier.n-check-quote.text.text: The quote must appear word for word in the document it names.

code-verifier.n-check-outdated.text.text: Copied word for word from d4 is still not allowed: the task's rule says it is out of date. The verifier always knows this rule.

code-verifier.n-check-gold.text.text: The documented values are in GOLD, the same for every run language.

code-verifier.n-check-answer.text.text: The correct option must state the documented value, and no other option may state it too.

code-verifier.n-verify.text.text: The runner calls it as a tool; all four modes use the same one.

code-verifier.n-verify-list.text.text: Without a list of questions it raises ValueError, which the platform turns into a structured error, so the run does not crash.

code-verifier.n-verify-group.text.text: Questions are grouped by topic; ones with an unknown topic are counted in unmatched.

code-verifier.n-verify-topics.text.text: Each topic is judged in turn, giving one check per topic in the lab report.

code-verifier.n-verify-missing.text.text: No question for a topic, or more than one, fails the whole topic.

code-verifier.n-verify-return.text.text: Task acceptance passes only when all three topics pass.

code-decision.title.text: The program as manager, an optional rule in the handoff, one verifier at the end

code-decision.chosen.text: All four modes share one task, one set of documents and one program verifier; for the independent agents, the program does the split and the merge in a fixed way, whether the handoff package carries the rule is a parameter, and the merge only records duplicates and conflicts without deciding; every call records its run identity and what its context really held.

code-decision.model-manager.title.text: Let a model act as manager and decide how many researchers to send

code-decision.model-manager.why_not.text: Dynamic splitting was covered in {{lesson:orchestrator-evaluator}}; this lesson compares how context is divided, and only a fixed split lets the difference be traced to context.

code-decision.merge-resolves.title.text: Have the program drop the facts from d4 at the merge by rule

code-decision.merge-resolves.why_not.text: That would hide the rule inside the merge code and conceal that the handoff package lost information; this lesson only records the conflict and lets the consequence show up in the verifier.

code-decision.reviewer-accepts.title.text: Use the reviewer's verdict as the acceptance result

code-decision.reviewer-accepts.why_not.text: What the reviewer sees may be incomplete; acceptance goes to a program that knows the full rules, which keeps the four modes comparable.

code-decision.graph-framework.title.text: Write the four modes with a graph framework

code-decision.graph-framework.why_not.text: {{lesson:langgraph-state}} covered graph frameworks; here plain Python keeps the context of every request in plain view.

four-modes.title.text: Comparing modes for research, writing and review

four-modes.hypothesis.text: The four modes do the same question-writing task and are judged by the same verifier; the finer the split, the more model calls, and usually more input characters, though not strictly in step (role switching grows its context round by round); parallel researchers let the waiting overlap, but the number of topics that pass the verifier does not grow just because there are more roles, and a single agent can fail a topic through how its options are worded.

four-modes.context.text.text: What the context of the first model call really held: number of messages, input characters, documents seen, whether the old-draft rule was there.

four-modes.identities.text.text: How many run identities and how many roles this run had.

four-modes.verifier-call.text.text: The runner initiates the verifier call; all four modes use the same tool.

four-modes.task.text.text: Task acceptance: how many of the three topics passed.

four-modes.tokens.text.text: Total total_tokens, only numbers the provider reported.

four-modes.wall.text.text: Wall-clock time measured on the backend.

four-modes.guide.0.text.text: All four modes do the same task: four documents, three topics, one verifier. First look at what each call's context held.

four-modes.guide.1.text.text: The single agent's first call sees all documents and the rule; an independent researcher sees only its own shard.

four-modes.guide.2.text.text: Role switching has 1 run identity and 3 roles; the independent agents have 5 run identities.

four-modes.guide.3.text.text: The final questions go to the same verifier, and the runner made this call; the model did not propose it.

four-modes.guide.4.text.text: Task acceptance: compare only results from the same verifier.

four-modes.guide.5.text.text: The four modes make 1, 3, 3 and 5 model calls, and parallelism does not reduce that.

four-modes.guide.6.text.text: Usage adds up only the total_tokens the provider reported; nothing unreported is estimated.

four-modes.guide.7.text.text: The independent researchers run in parallel, so this stretch of the wall-clock time overlaps; the writer and reviewer still wait one after the other, and in these runs the total came out longer than for the single agent and the fixed workflow.

four-modes.conclusion.proves.0.text: This run's results for the four modes on the same task and verifier: how many topics passed, the number of model calls, the reported usage and the wall-clock time, plus what each call's context really held.

four-modes.conclusion.does_not_prove.0.text: One run cannot show which mode is better; run each several times before comparing.

four-modes.conclusion.does_not_prove.1.text: The verifier only checks the evidence and the documented values; whether the questions are good still needs a person to read them.

four-modes.conclusion.does_not_prove.2.text: In offline test mode the replies, usage and timing come from a fixed script and do not represent any real model.

handoff-loss.title.text: A handoff package that leaves out one rule

handoff-loss.hypothesis.text: With the minimal handoff, the researcher assigned the old draft does not know it is out of date; the merge shows duplicated work and a contradiction, and the error may travel all the way to the verifier. With the rule in the handoff package the conflict disappears and every request's input grows.

handoff-loss.branch.text.text: Each researcher's request carries its own branch.

handoff-loss.old-draft.text.text: The researcher whose context holds the old draft d4.

handoff-loss.rule.text.text: Whether the researcher's context holds the rule that d4 is out of date.

handoff-loss.merge.text.text: The contradiction recorded at the merge: one topic, different values and their sources.

handoff-loss.worker-check.text.text: The verifier's verdict on the subtask-limit question.

handoff-loss.input.text.text: Total input characters across all requests.

handoff-loss.guide.0.text.text: Both arms are independent agents; they differ only in whether the handoff package has the rule that d4 is out of date.

handoff-loss.guide.1.text.text: The three researchers' requests go out at the same time, and the timeline pairs requests and responses by branch.

handoff-loss.guide.2.text.text: researcher-3 was assigned d3 and d4, so its context holds the old draft.

handoff-loss.guide.3.text.text: Now the rule: false in the minimal arm, true in the arm with rules.

handoff-loss.guide.4.text.text: At the merge, conflicts in the minimal arm lists two values for worker_cap; in the arm with rules it is an empty list.

handoff-loss.guide.5.text.text: The verifier's verdict on this question shows whether the error travelled all the way to the end.

handoff-loss.guide.6.text.text: The price: with rules every request carries an extra paragraph, so the total input characters are higher.

handoff-loss.conclusion.proves.0.text: Whether the handoff package has that rule decides whether the researchers' contexts have it; duplicates and conflicts at the merge and the verifier's verdict can all be found in the events.

handoff-loss.conclusion.does_not_prove.0.text: Without the rule the offline script always takes the later fact; a real model may choose right or wrong.

handoff-loss.conclusion.does_not_prove.1.text: Adding the rule to the handoff package removed this one conflict; it does not mean other omissions in a handoff are gone.

inputs.handoff.help.text: Only affects the independent agents: the minimal handoff gives only the task and the assigned documents; with rules it also adds the rule that d4 is out of date.

quiz.q1.prompt.text: How can you tell that a system really has several independent agents, rather than one agent that switched roles several times?

quiz.q1.a.text.text: Check whether the contexts are separate, the available tools differ and the run identities differ

quiz.q1.a.feedback.text: Right. Only when these three are separate are the agents independent.

quiz.q1.b.text.text: Count the role names written in the system prompts

quiz.q1.b.feedback.text: No. Role switching writes several role names too.

quiz.q1.c.text.text: Count how many times the model was called

quiz.q1.c.feedback.text: No. The fixed workflow and role switching both make 3 calls.

quiz.q1.explanation.text: Role switching only swaps the system prompt; neither the context nor the run identity is separated.

quiz.q2.prompt.text: With the minimal handoff, researcher-3 reported the value from d4. Why?

quiz.q2.a.text.text: Its context has d4 but not the rule that d4 is out of date

quiz.q2.a.feedback.text: Right. The rule is only in the task description, and the minimal handoff did not pass it on.

quiz.q2.b.text.text: It saw the other researchers' results and followed them

quiz.q2.b.feedback.text: No. The researchers cannot see each other.

quiz.q2.c.feedback.text: No. The verifier always checks against the full rules.

quiz.q2.explanation.text: Context isolation loses whatever was not handed over.

quiz.q3.prompt.text: merge_facts finds two different values for worker_cap. What does the program do?

quiz.q3.a.text.text: It records them in conflicts of lesson.merge, decides nothing for the researchers, and passes every fact to the writer

quiz.q3.a.feedback.text: Right. The program only records, and the consequence shows up in the verifier.

quiz.q3.b.text.text: It automatically drops the fact from d4

quiz.q3.b.feedback.text: No. That would hide the rule inside the merge code.

quiz.q3.c.text.text: It sends another researcher to look again

quiz.q3.c.feedback.text: No. This lesson's merge never adds calls.

quiz.q3.explanation.text: The merge only records duplicates and conflicts; it does not decide.

quiz.q4.prompt.text: Three researchers run in parallel, each request takes 2 seconds, and nothing queues before or after. Roughly how long does the research stretch take, and how many model calls are there?

quiz.q4.a.feedback.text: Right. The waiting overlaps; not a single call is saved.

quiz.q4.b.feedback.text: No. In parallel the three requests wait at the same time, and each request is one call.

quiz.q4.c.feedback.text: No. Parallelism does not merge three requests into one.

quiz.q4.explanation.text: Parallelism saves time, not calls or usage.

quiz.q5.prompt.text: The independent agents and the single agent both passed the verifier, and the multi-agent mode made 4 more calls. What should you conclude?

quiz.q5.a.text.text: This run shows no evidence that the split pays off, so a single agent is fine; to be surer, run each several times

quiz.q5.a.feedback.text: Right. A gain has to be shown on the same task with the same verifier.

quiz.q5.b.text.text: The multi-agent mode is more reliable because it has a reviewer

quiz.q5.b.feedback.text: No. A reviewer that brings no new information only adds calls.

quiz.q5.c.text.text: Both are equally good, so use multiple agents from now on

quiz.q5.c.feedback.text: No. When both are equally good, the cheaper one is the better fit.

quiz.q5.explanation.text: The number of roles is not a measure of capability; extra calls must be paid for by a gain.

quiz.q6.prompt.text: Which kind of collaboration is most likely to bring information a single agent cannot get?

quiz.q6.a.text.text: A reviewer reviewing code with the results of running its tests

quiz.q6.a.feedback.text: Right. Test results did not exist when the code was written.

quiz.q6.b.text.text: The same model rereading its own output under another identity

quiz.q6.b.feedback.text: No. It still sees the same things.

quiz.q6.c.text.text: Two agents debating the same piece of text

quiz.q6.c.feedback.text: No. Without outside feedback, debate is usually no better than a single agent.

quiz.q6.explanation.text: Whether collaboration is worth it depends on whether it brings in new information.

check-hunt.prompt.text: Run "Independent agents" and find the evidence where the merge recorded a contradiction.

check-hunt.explanation.text: lesson.merge is recorded when the program merges the facts, after all three researchers have returned and before the writer starts. With the minimal handoff, conflicts contains worker_cap: researcher-2 reported 4 from d2 and researcher-3 reported 6 from d4; duplicates contains worker_cap too, showing that both looked up the same topic. Run again with the handoff with rules and both lists are empty.

check-points.prompt.text: Compare with your own runs and this lesson's source, and tick an item once you have done it.

check-points.item-1.text.text: I ran all four modes and compared the verdicts, the number of model calls, the total usage and the wall-clock time.

check-points.item-2.text.text: I found the shared message history in the role-switching mode and the separate branches in the independent-agents mode.

check-points.item-3.text.text: I ran the independent agents once with each handoff package and can say how researcher-3's context differs.

code_notes.lesson.agent.note.text: Recorded after each model call: run identity, role, branch, and how many messages, which documents and whether the rule were in the context.

code_notes.lesson.merge.note.text: Recorded when the independent agents' facts are merged: every fact, topics researched twice, topics with contradicting values.

code_notes.outdated_docs.note.text: A lesson.agent field that appears only when the context holds the old draft, listing which documents.

code_notes.sees_rule.note.text: Whether the context holds the rule that d4 is out of date, read from the messages actually sent.

code_notes.handoff.note.text: Parameter: minimal passes only the task and assigned documents, with_rules adds the rule; it only affects independent agents.

code_notes.merge_facts.note.text: Collects facts in researcher order and records topics researched twice or with different values, deciding nothing.

code_notes.verify_quiz.note.text: The program verifier all four modes share; the runner calls it as a tool and judges each topic.

code_notes.branch.note.text: The pairing tag for parallel requests; this lesson uses the researcher's run identity, such as researcher-3.

code_notes.worker_cap.note.text: Topic: the orchestrator's subtask limit. d2 says 4, the old draft d4 says 6.

code_notes.d4.note.text: Extra notes whose title does not look old; only the rule in the task description says it is out of date.

code_notes.assistant.note.text: The only run identity in the role-switching mode, used by all three stages.

code_notes.quote.note.text: The exact text in a question's evidence; it must appear word for word in the document named by doc.

code_notes.GOLD.note.text: Each topic's value in the current documents: other, 4, 3, the same in every run language.
